topics.title: The Second 'Aqabah Pledge

paragraphs.text: The next year, the thirteenth of Prophethood (June 622 A.D.), during the pilgrimage season, over seventy converts from Madinah came in the trail of their polytheist people to perform the rituals of pilgrimage in Makkah. The oft-repeated question amongst them was: "Isn't it high time we protect Muhammad instead of leaving him forsaken, deserted and stumbling in the hillocks of Makkah?" Shortly after arrival, they conducted clandestine contacts with the Prophet (Peace be upon him) and agreed to meet him secretly at night in mid Tashreeq Days (the 11th, 12th and 13th of Dhul Hijja) in a hillock at Al-'Aqabah, the previous year's meeting place.

Ka'b bin Malik Al-Ansari (May Allah be pleased with him) gave an account of that historic meeting: "We set out for pilgrimage and struck a rendezvous in mid Tashreeq Days. We were accompanied by a notable of ours called 'Abdullah bin 'Amr bin Haram, who was still a polytheist. We disclosed to him our intention of meeting Muhammad (Peace be upon him) and exhorted him to give up polytheism lest he should serve as wood for Hell. He promptly embraced Islam and witnessed the meeting at Al-'Aqabah. That very night we slept with our people in our camps. After a third of the night had elapsed, we began to leave stealthily and met in a hillock nearby. We were seventy-three men and two women — Nusaibah bint Ka'b from the Najjars and Asma' bint 'Amr from Bani Salamah."

We waited for the Messenger of Allah (Peace be upon him) until he came in the company of his uncle Al-'Abbas bin 'Abdul Muttalib who, though himself not a Muslim, was the first to speak: "O you people of the Khazraj, you all know the position that Muhammad holds among us. We have protected him from our people as much as we could. He is honoured and respected among his people, and refuses to join any party except you. So if you think you can carry out what you promise while inviting him to your town, and defend him against his enemies, then assume the burden you have taken. But if you are going to surrender and betray him after having taken him away with you, you had better leave him now, because he is respected and well defended in his own place." Ka'b replied: "We have heard your words, and now, O Messenger of Allah, it is for you to speak and take from us any pledge that you want regarding your Lord and yourself."

The Messenger of Allah then preached the Faith, and the pledge was taken. On the authority of Jabir, the Ansâr asked the Messenger of Allah about the principles over which they would take a pledge. The Prophet answered: "To listen and obey in all sets of circumstances; to spend in plenty as well as in scarcity; to enjoin good and forbid evil; in Allah's service, you will fear the censure of none; to defend me in case I seek your help, and debar me from anything you debar yourself, your spouses and children from. And if you observe those precepts, Paradise is in store for you."

In another version narrated by Ka'b, the Prophet (Peace be upon him) recited some Qur'ânic verses, called people unto Allah, and concluded: "I give you my pledge that you debar me from whatever you debar your women and children from." Al-Bara' bin Ma'rur caught him by the hand and said: "Oh yes, we swear by Allah, Who sent you as a Prophet in Truth, that we will debar you from whatever we debar our women from. We are genuine fighters and quite reliable in war, a trait passed down to us from our ancestors." Then Abul Haitham At-Taihan interrupted: "O Prophet of Allah! Between us and the Jews there are agreements which we would then sever. If Allah grants you power and victory, should we expect that you would not leave us and rejoin your own people?" The Prophet (Peace be upon him) smiled and replied: "Nay, it would never be; your blood will be my blood. In life and death I will be with you and you with me. I will fight whom you fight and I will make peace with those with whom you make peace."

Al-'Abbas bin 'Ubadah bin Nadlah then remarked: "O you people of Khazraj! Do you know the significance of the pact you are entering into with this man? You are avowing that you will fight against all and sundry. If you fear that your property will be at stake or the lives of your nobles endangered, then leave him now, because if you do this after the pledge it will be degrading for you in this world and the next. But if you think you can carry it out in spite of the loss of lives and property, then undertake this responsibility, for herein lies the good of this world and the next." They replied: "We have already considered the loss of property and the murder of our notables, yet we pay him allegiance. But what is our reward if we observe all the items of this pact?" The Prophet replied: "Paradise." They stretched out their hands and took the pledge.

On the authority of Jabir: when they started to pay allegiance, As'ad bin Zurarah stood up and said: "Take it easy, people of Yathrib! We have not covered that long distance except because we have deep belief that he is the Messenger of Allah. We are already convinced that following him entails departure from the pagan Arabs even at the risk of our lives. Should you persevere in this course, your great reward is with Allah; but if you are caught in fear, give it up now, and then you would be more excusable before Allah." With respect to the two women, the pledge was taken orally, for the Prophet (Peace be upon him) had never shaken hands with a strange lady.

The Prophet (Peace be upon him) then asked the group to appoint twelve deputies to preach Islam to their people and oversee the articles of the pledge. Nine were from Al-Khazraj: As'ad bin Zurarah, Sa'd bin Ar-Rabi', 'Abdullah bin Rawahah, Rafi' bin Malik, Al-Bara' bin Ma'rur, 'Abdullah bin 'Amr bin Haram, 'Ubadah bin As-Samit, Sa'd bin 'Ubadah and Al-Mundhir bin 'Amr. Three were from Al-Aws: Usaid bin Hudair, Sa'd bin Khaithamah and Rifa'a bin 'Abdul Mundhir. Those twelve were sworn to act as surety over the affairs of their people, just as Christ's disciples did, while the Prophet would act as surety over all the Muslims.

Somehow the news of these secret meetings leaked out. On hearing this, Al-'Abbas bin Nadlah said: "By Allah, Who has sent you in Truth, we are powerful enough to put the people of Mina (the Quraishites) to our swords tomorrow, if you desire." The Prophet (Peace be upon him) said: "We have not been commanded to follow that course. Now, back to your camps." The next day, a large delegation of Makkan leaders set out to protest to the Madinese: "O people of Khazraj, it transpired to us that you have come to conclude a treaty with this man and evacuate him out of Makkah..." The Madinese polytheists, knowing nothing of the secret pledge, swore in good faith that there was no truth in the report; 'Abdullah bin Ubai bin Salul also denied it. The Quraishites went back frustrated, but later established beyond doubt that the pact had indeed taken place — after the pilgrims had left. They pursued them and caught only Sa'd bin 'Ubadah, whom they tortured until he was rescued by Al-Mut'im bin 'Adi and Harith bin Harb.

That is the story of the Second 'Aqabah Pledge, later known as the Great 'Aqabah Pledge, effected in an atmosphere of love, allegiance and mutual support between the Madinese believers and the weak Makkan Muslims. This spirit of affection and cooperation derived not from a passing whim but from a deeply-established faith — Belief in Allah, His Messenger and His Book — so rooted that it stood immune to all powers of injustice and could be translated into miracles in action. That Belief was the real instrument by which the Muslims recorded unprecedented breakthroughs in the annals of history.

topics.topicSummary: In the thirteenth year, over seventy Madinese believers met the Prophet ﷺ secretly at Al-'Aqabah during the pilgrimage. Introduced by his uncle Al-'Abbas, they pledged to listen, obey, spend, enjoin good, and defend the Prophet ﷺ as they would their own women and children — for the reward of Paradise. The Prophet ﷺ vowed his blood was their blood, and appointed twelve deputies. When the news leaked, Quraish protested and later tortured Sa'd bin 'Ubadah. This Great Pledge, born of deep faith, set the stage for the Hijrah.
keyPoints: Over seventy Madinese converts met the Prophet ﷺ secretly at Al-'Aqabah in the thirteenth year (622 A.D.)
73 men and 2 women (Nusaibah bint Ka'b and Asma' bint 'Amr) attended
His uncle Al-'Abbas spoke first, warning them of the burden of protecting the Prophet ﷺ
They pledged to listen, obey, spend, enjoin good, and defend him as they would their own families
The Prophet ﷺ vowed: 'your blood will be my blood... I will fight whom you fight'
Twelve deputies (nine Khazraj, three Aws) were appointed as sureties over their people
Quraish discovered the pact, protested to the Madinese, and tortured Sa'd bin 'Ubadah
This 'Great 'Aqabah Pledge' set the stage for the migration to Madinah

quiz.question: Approximately how many Madinese took part in the Second 'Aqabah Pledge?
Who introduced the gathering by warning the Ansar of the responsibility, though not yet a Muslim?
How many deputies (nuqaba') did the Prophet ﷺ appoint over the Madinese?
Which Madinese was captured and tortured by Quraish after the pledge?
